title: Proof by Cases
short: Split into cases that cover every possibility (n even or odd; n = 3k, 3k + 1 or 3k + 2) and prove each one.
trouble: Students leave out a case, such as zero or the negative numbers.

blocks.html: Some claims are easy once you know a little more about the number: whether it is even or odd, or what remainder it leaves. A proof by cases splits the problem so that each piece is a short direct proof.

To prove $Q$ by cases, list cases $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots$ that together cover every possibility, then prove that each case leads to $Q$. Standard splits: $n$ even or odd ($n = 2k$ or $2k + 1$); remainders when dividing by $3$ ($n = 3k$, $3k + 1$ or $3k + 2$); signs ($x > 0$, $x = 0$, $x < 0$).

Logically, $(C_{1} \vee C_{2})$, $C_{1} \to Q$ and $C_{2} \to Q$ together give $Q$: whichever case actually happens, $Q$ follows. The argument is only as good as the first fact, that the cases cover everything. Every integer leaves a remainder of $0$, $1$ or $2$ when divided by $3$, so the three forms $3k$, $3k + 1$, $3k + 2$ really do cover all integers.

blocks.title: $n^{2} + n$ is always even
blocks.q: Prove: for every integer $n$, $n^{2} + n$ is even.
steps: Every integer is even or odd, so the cases cover everything.

blocks.title: Squares and the number $3$
blocks.q: Prove: for every integer $n$, $n^{2}$ leaves remainder $0$ or $1$ when divided by $3$.
steps: So a perfect square never leaves remainder $2$. (That is why, for example, $3m + 2$ is never a perfect square.)

blocks.title: Absolute values
blocks.q: Prove: for all real numbers $x$ and $y$, $|xy| = |x|\,|y|$.
steps: Case $x \ge 0, y < 0$: $xy \le 0$, so $|xy| = -xy = x(-y) = |x|\,|y|$. The case $x < 0, y \ge 0$ is the same with the roles swapped.
blocks.a: True in all four sign cases.

blocks.html: Leaving out a case. A proof that checks "$x > 0$" and "$x < 0$" has skipped $x = 0$; a proof about integers that only handles positive $n$ has skipped zero and the negatives. Check: before writing any case, ask whether every possible value lands in at least one case. For remainder cases, list one remainder for each value from $0$ to the divisor minus $1$.
